title: Strip slash-command markup from titles
description:
42 conversations (1.4%) show garbage as their result header — harness-injected markup
reaching the title verbatim instead of the prose the user actually typed. Examples:
`find-skills` from a slash-command expansion, a sentence about whichever file happened to be
focused in the editor, and bracketed interruption notices the harness writes as though the
user had typed them.

Both importer paths are affected and they need different rules, because the two tools inject
differently: Claude Code wraps machinery in pseudo-XML tags, Codex writes bare slash-command
lines and `[$name](path)` skill links.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `cs index`
2. `cs search` with a blank query to list recent conversations, or search for `find-skills`.
3. Scan the grouped result headers. 42 of them are markup rather than prose — a
   slash-command expansion, an `ide_opened_file` sentence, or `[Request interrupted by user]`.

Blocks the eval set (chat-search-6eb.9): a result header that shows machinery makes
"is this the conversation I meant" unanswerable, so relevance judgements would be scored
against a title the ranking never saw.
acceptance_criteria: No conversation title on either the claude-code or codex path contains harness-injected markup. A turn that is entirely markup yields no title and the next user message gets the job. <command-args> keeps its body when the sibling <command-name> is a custom command and yields nothing when it is /model or /fast. Bare bracketed harness notices never title a conversation. Codex bare slash-command lines are rejected while real paths (/Users/x, /usr/local/bin) and prose containing a slash are not. All 42 affected conversations render real prose. Synthetic tests only.
close_reason: Verified against a fresh full-corpus index: 0 conversation titles contain pseudo-XML markup, ide_* blocks, bracketed harness notices, or bare slash commands. Both importer paths covered by synthetic tests.

title: ymd() renders dates in UTC, so evening-local conversations show tomorrow date
description:
A session at 2026-07-18 21:00 PDT prints as 2026-07-19. Every grouped result line is
affected, and a wrong date makes "is this the one I meant" unanswerable.

Not a rare edge: `ymd()` renders in UTC, so on Pacific time every conversation after 17:00
local shows tomorrow's date — roughly seven hours of every day, and the evening is when a
lot of this corpus was written.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Find a conversation whose `ended_at` is an evening local time — 2026-07-18 21:00 PDT is
   2026-07-19 04:00 UTC.
2. `cs index`, then `cs search` for it.
3. The grouped result header reads 2026-07-19. It should read 2026-07-18.
design:
DECIDED: take chrono, convert to local at the parse boundary, keep storage as epoch millis.

Rationale from fast-resume (the category leader, already benchmarked against): it depends on chrono 0.4 and uses Local exclusively — Utc appears nowhere in its src/. Adapters convert at parse time (adapters/shared.rs parse_datetime returns DateTime<Local> via with_timezone(&Local), with a naive-local fallback for offset-less formats), then reduce to f64 epoch seconds for storage. Local-ness is a render/bucket concern, never a storage one — which matches ended_at already being epoch millis here.

Rejected: reading TZ or /etc/localtime for a fixed offset. Correct for ymd() today, wrong the moment date arithmetic appears. fast-resume's next_day_start_seconds uses checked_add_days(Days::new(1)) — civil-day arithmetic — and its test proves a next-day boundary is 82,800s across spring-forward and 90,000s across fall-back, neither of which a fixed offset can express. chat-search-6eb.11 (Query DSL) would want exactly this for after:/before:/yesterday filters.

Testing note: fast-resume keeps chrono-tz as a DEV-dependency only, to pin a zone (Europe/Paris) so DST behaviour is deterministic in tests. Production reads the system zone. Worth copying.

The old localtime_r advisory does not apply — chrono 0.4 has not pulled in time 0.1 by default for years.
acceptance_criteria: Dates render as the local civil date: a conversation at 2026-07-18 21:00 PDT prints 2026-07-18. Storage stays epoch millis — local-ness is a render concern, never a storage one. A test pins the behaviour against a fixed zone via chrono-tz as a dev-dependency only, so it is deterministic in CI regardless of the runner's zone. The rule lives in exactly one place, landing as part of chat-search-me9.12 rather than separately, so ymd() in the binary and the strflocaltime call in the cs-fzf jq both go away.
close_reason: Landed as part of me9.12. cs-core/src/time.rs owns the rule; DST behaviour pinned with chrono-tz as a dev-dependency; Group.ended_date rendered in cs-core so no client re-derives it.

title: ChatGPT reaches the index only via --chatgpt-export
description:
69% of the corpus vanishes silently if the flag is omitted. An eval run without it measures
the wrong index and nothing says so.

The ChatGPT export is the only source not read through `ArchiveReader` — `crates/cs/src/query.rs:63-79`
reads it straight from a directory handed in on the command line, which is why it is the one
source that can be forgotten.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `cs index` with no flags.
2. `cs search` for a phrase you know is in a ChatGPT conversation.
3. Zero hits. The run reports success and its per-source table simply has no
   `chatgpt-export` row — nothing states that 2,011 conversations were not considered.
4. `cs index --chatgpt-export ~/dev/sandbox/chat-history/data/`, search again, and the same
   phrase is found.
acceptance_criteria: ChatGPT conversations are indexed on a default run with no extra flags, or the run refuses to proceed and says what is missing.
close_reason: chatgpt-export is now an ordinary mirror source in config.toml and the --chatgpt-export flag is gone; a bare 'cs index' reaches all 2,011 ChatGPT conversations. Also closes the silent half of the acceptance: a configured source the archive holds nothing for now gets a report row stating why (bundle-not-implemented vs nothing-archived) instead of being skipped invisibly — opencode now shows as skipped rather than absent.

title: Log what was searched for and what was opened
description: Ground truth the eval set cannot invent. 'cs search' appends query + returned ids + latency; 'cs pick <conv_id> --query <text>' appends the selection with its rank; 'cs needs' folds the log into one row per distinct query. cs-fzf carries conv_id as a hidden field and calls 'cs pick' on selection.
design:
Log at <archive_root>/queries.jsonl, append-only. Deliberately NOT in index.db: index.db is a pure function of the archive and can be deleted at will, while this cannot be reconstructed from anything and wants backing up. First authored data the project keeps, and the first thing that will move into library.db (chat-search-6eb.14).

Typeahead is excluded — '--prefix' fires once per keystroke, so logging it would bury the handful of real queries under every prefix of each. Clients doing typeahead record the finished query via 'cs pick' instead, which is why cs-fzf uses fzf's --print-query.

'cs pick' recomputes the result list rather than being handed it, because the caller is a shell script holding one chosen line. Costs a few ms and keeps the recorded rank honest about what the ranking would actually return.

A pick with rank=None is kept, not dropped: it means the conversation was reached some other way, and discarding those would bias the log toward things that already ranked well.

Writes never fail the operation they describe — a search that cannot write its log line still returns results.
acceptance_criteria: Searches and picks are recorded; 'cs needs' shows queries with their picks and ranks; log_queries=false in config suppresses everything; a corrupt line costs that line and not the history.
close_reason: Landed 2026-07-30. cs-core/src/querylog.rs (Event, append, load, needs — 6 synthetic tests), Config::query_log() + log_queries, 'cs pick', 'cs needs', search logging in query.rs, cs-fzf wired via --print-query and a hidden conv_id field. Verified end to end against the real index: rank-3 pick recorded as rank=3, opt-out honoured.

title: Preview pane: fold model, collapsed tool traffic, outline mode
description:
The preview is what answers 'is this the one I meant', and it is a separable chunk of chat-search-me9.1 rather than a detail of it. Spec: docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §7.

Renders from message rows, never from a flattened blob — we have role, kind, seq, parent_id, on_head_path, so none of fast-resume's prose-sniffing heuristics are needed (it splits on blank lines and guesses role from a '» ' prefix, which loses the role on every multi-paragraph user message).

Three pieces:

1. **Fold model.** Every message becomes a block with a collapsed form (1-2 lines) and an expanded form. Fold::Auto resolves against (density, kind); an explicit per-message override wins. This subsumes tool collapsing, reasoning collapsing and outline mode into one mechanism instead of three special cases.

2. **Tool traffic collapsed by default, not hidden.** Tool text is 91% of the corpus (ADR 5), so collapsing is what makes the pane readable — but that a tool ran is recognition information, so it stays as a one-line affordance. A tool message that matched fts_tools expands, which is how a tool-field hit becomes visible rather than mysterious. A failed tool_result stays legible collapsed, in the error colour.

3. **Outline mode.** Collapses every turn including prose to one line, two for the focused message. At a 36-line preview that is the whole conversation for most of this corpus. Because collapsed prose prefers the *matching* line, outline mode doubles as a match map — every hit across the conversation, in sequence order, complementary to the top-3 hit rows which are in rank order.

Also: read messages on selection change rather than carrying text on the row struct, and cache blocks keyed on (conv_id, query, density, fold overrides) rather than rebuilding per frame — fast-resume rebuilds the whole preview including syntax highlighting on every render tick (render.rs:769).
design:
Block { msg_id, role, kind, on_path, collapsed: Vec<Line>, expanded: Vec<Line> }, with Fold { Auto, Collapsed, Expanded } per message and Density { Full, Outline } pane-wide. Blocks carry provenance (which message, on-path or not) because the off-path branch display needs it — see docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §7.

No hand-rolled syntax highlighting. fast-resume spends ~150 lines on it and it is barely language-aware — the keyword list is a flat union across languages, so 'def' highlights inside JavaScript. Render fenced blocks dim, keep the match highlight applied inside them, stop.

Keymap constraint: the search box consumes every unmodified keystroke, so each command costs a modifier. Ctrl+O cycles density; the per-message fold override needs a second key and that choice is still open.

Depends on chat-search-6eb.20: highlighting must come from the same tokenizer that ranked, or a stemmed hit highlights nothing.
acceptance_criteria: Preview renders from a message-row query, not a parsed blob; a multi-paragraph user message keeps its role throughout. Tool calls and results render as one collapsed line by default, expand on override, and auto-expand when the hit came from fts_tools. A failed tool result is legible while collapsed. Outline mode collapses every turn to one line and prefers the matching line, so every hit in the conversation is visible on one screen. Blocks are built once per (conv, query, density, folds), not per frame. Match highlighting agrees with the ranker on a stemmed query.

title: snippet() substring-matches a Porter-stemmed index, so stemmed hits show the wrong text
description:
fts_prose and fts_tools tokenize with `porter unicode61 remove_diacritics 2` (crates/cs-core/src/schema.rs:54-57), but snippet() locates the match with a raw substring scan — `lower.find(t)` at crates/cs-core/src/search.rs:93. The two disagree for every term whose stem differs from the literal text in the message.

When find() misses, `at` is None, start falls back to 0, and the leading ellipsis is omitted (search.rs:97-107) — so the snippet renders the first 160 chars of the message as though that were the match site. It looks like a deliberate summary, not a fallback. Wrong output presented as correct output.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Index a conversation whose prose reads `Commit current changes`.
2. `cs search commits` — Porter stems both `commits` and `commit` to `commit`, so the row ranks and appears.
3. The snippet shows the head of the message with no ellipsis, and the matching word is not in it. Same for `learning` against text containing `learned`, and any plural/gerund/past-tense pair.
4. `remove_diacritics 2` adds a smaller case: query `cafe` matches text `café`, find() does not.

The existing test only covers a literal exact term (`snippet_centres_on_the_first_matching_term`, search.rs:303), which is why this is uncovered.

## Also wrong: the term set

snippet() splits the raw query string, so once the query DSL lands (chat-search-6eb.11) `agent:codex learning` contributes `agent` and `codex` as snippet anchors. fast-resume already solved this — see is_search_filter_token in its tui/preview.rs:462-467. Strip filter tokens before deriving snippet terms.

Blocks any correct match highlighting in the TUI preview (chat-search-me9.1), and chat-search-6eb.10 fuzzy-on-failure would make it total: a fuzzy hit never substring-matches.
design:
Contentless fts5 rules out the SQL snippet() and highlight() auxiliary functions — they need reconstructable content — so hand-rolling is forced, not a shortcut. The fix is to match at token level with the same rules the index uses: tokenize the message text (unicode61 + diacritic folding), Porter-stem each token, and mark tokens whose stem is in the query's stem set. That yields both the anchor position and the highlight spans from one pass, and it stays correct when fuzzy matching lands (compare edit distance on stems rather than raw text).

Anchor on the best match rather than the earliest. Both this code and fast-resume take min(position), so one incidental early mention beats the dense cluster later in a long conversation. search_grouped already ranks per message before grouping, so the best-hit message is known at hydrate time — use it.
acceptance_criteria: A query whose term stems to a different surface form than the text renders a snippet centred on the actual matching token, with the token marked. Filter keywords from the query DSL never act as snippet anchors. A snippet that genuinely cannot locate a match says so rather than silently rendering the head of the message. Tests cover a plural, a gerund, and a diacritic case, not only a literal exact term.
notes:
Weight increased 2026-07-30 without the bug changing. The eval sheet (chat-search-6eb.9) shows exactly one snippet per candidate as the primary evidence for a grade — the design deliberately chose one accurate snippet plus a match-position strip over three noisy ones. So a snippet that shows the wrong span for a stemmed hit no longer just looks scruffy in a result list; it means a relevance judgement gets made against text that is not what matched, and that judgement then becomes ground truth for tuning.

Same applies to the harvested log (chat-search-6eb.21): a pick is a vote cast on what the row showed.

Fix this before any serious judging pass.

title: Codex IDE context block leaks into 224 titles
description:
The Codex VS Code extension prepends a markdown context block to user turns — `# Context from my IDE setup:`
with `## Active file:`, `## Open tabs:`, and sometimes `## My request for Codex:` carrying the
real prose INSIDE it. It reaches the title verbatim on 198 conversations (6.7% of the
corpus). A related `# Files mentioned by the user:` block accounts for 26 more. 224 total.

Found while fixing chat-search-n58.3, which covered a different and smaller set (5 patterns,
37 conversations, 1.3%). This is 5x the blast radius of that bug.

Not pseudo-XML and not slash-command markup, so neither the claude_code strip_injected_markup
literal tag scan nor the new codex is_command_line/unwrap_skill_links handles it. Needs its
own rule: a markdown-heading-structured prelude, where the useful prose may be nested under a
`## My request for Codex:` subheading rather than following the block.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `cs index`
2. `cs search` with a blank query to list recent conversations, or search for
   `Context from my IDE setup`.
3. 198 conversation headers begin with `# Context from my IDE setup:` followed by
   `## Active file:` / `## Open tabs:`; 26 more begin with `# Files mentioned by the user:`.
   In the subset carrying `## My request for Codex:`, the prose that should have been the
   title is visible further down the same block.
design: Distinct from n58.3's patterns — deliberately left out of that fix rather than bolted on. The prelude is structured markdown, so the rule is heading-aware rather than tag-literal. Note the recovery case: when '## My request for Codex:' is present the real prose is inside the block, so this cannot simply drop the block wholesale the way DROPPED_TAGS does.
acceptance_criteria: No conversation title begins with '# Context from my IDE setup:' or '# Files mentioned by the user:'. Where '## My request for Codex:' is present, the title is the prose from inside it. Synthetic tests only.

title: Move client-shared helpers out of the cs binary into cs-core
description: default_db(), now_ms() and local date formatting all live in crates/cs/src/query.rs, but every client needs them. Any second client either duplicates them or reaches into the binary. The date rule already exists in three places: ymd() in the binary, a strflocaltime call in the cs-fzf jq, and implicitly in anything a future client writes. Prerequisite for the native TUI (chat-search-me9.1) and for any non-Rust client.
design: Move into cs-core (or cs-archive for the config-dependent path resolution). render_groups() deliberately stays in the binary: that is terminal presentation and the TUI wants its own. Fixing the UTC date bug (chat-search-6eb.8) should happen as part of this move rather than separately, so the corrected rule lands in one place instead of three.
acceptance_criteria: default_db(), now_ms() and local date formatting live in cs-core (or cs-archive for the config-dependent path resolution) and crates/cs/src/query.rs calls them rather than defining them. render_groups() deliberately stays in the binary — that is terminal presentation and the TUI wants its own. The date rule exists in exactly one place: ymd() in the binary and the strflocaltime call in the cs-fzf jq are both gone. The bundled chat-search-6eb.8 fix is included, so an evening-local conversation renders its local civil date. A second Rust client can link cs-core and get all three without touching the binary.
notes: Dependency call for the bundled 6eb.8 fix is DECIDED: chrono, converting to local at the parse boundary. Full rationale on chat-search-6eb.8's design field. Practical consequence for this move: the helper that lands in cs-core is a *formatting* function over an already-local DateTime, not a function that does timezone math — which is what lets the date rule genuinely live in one place instead of three.
close_reason: Verified: Config::default_db() in cs-archive, now_ms()/local_ymd()/ymd_in() in cs-core::time re-exported from cs-core, query.rs calls all three rather than defining them, render_groups() deliberately still in the binary, cs-fzf reads ended_date. Bundled 6eb.8 fix included.

title: fzf stopgap client for ranking evaluation
description: scripts/cs-fzf plus scripts/cs-fzf.sh. fzf used purely as a renderer: --disabled turns off its own filtering and change:reload re-runs cs search per keystroke, so ranking stays ours. Exists to make the eval set (chat-search-6eb.9) practical to build long before a native TUI lands. Measured 8-26 ms per keystroke on a 168k-message index, of which 1.4-6.4 ms is the query and the rest is spawning cs and jq.
design: Launching the agent from inside the script proved fragile: fzf stdin is a pipe, and both become() and a plain exec left Claude Code unable to read keystrokes and Codex panicking in crossterm with "reader source not set". Final shape prints the command on stdout and lets the caller run it — csf() as a sourced shell function, or --run for a direct exec with no shell in between. ChatGPT rows resume via a URL rather than a command, so fmt rewrites those to open "<url>"; that rewrite is a workaround living in jq and should be deleted once chat-search-me9.3 lands.
close_reason: Shipped scripts/cs-fzf and scripts/cs-fzf.sh. Opens on recent conversations, live search per keystroke, csf() and --run both verified under a pty to give the launched agent a tty on all three fds.

title: Synthetic golden-file fixtures
description: A Codex subagent thread, a declared fork, a renamed session, a ChatGPT edit-branch. Must be synthetic: real transcripts contain secrets, and without them the repo can never be shared.
design: Hand-authored, not captured-and-scrubbed. Scrubbing a real transcript leaves you asserting that you found every secret, which is unfalsifiable and only has to be wrong once; authoring from scratch makes the claim structural. Keep each fixture minimal — the smallest file that still exhibits the structure under test — so a golden diff points at one behaviour instead of a wall of noise. These are the fixtures every other parser bug (chat-search-n58.6, n58.7, n58.13, n58.14) will need, so shape them for reuse rather than per-issue.
acceptance_criteria: Fixtures exist for a Codex subagent thread, a declared fork, a renamed session, and a ChatGPT edit-branch, each with a golden expected-output file. Every byte is synthetic — a grep of the fixture tree for real paths, hostnames, API-key shapes and the machine UUID returns nothing. Each importer's test suite runs against them, and a deliberate regression in the importer fails the golden diff rather than passing silently.

title: resume_cmd is the wrong shape for open it somewhere
description: It is a string format!ed inside each importer and frozen into a column, so it can express exactly one way to reopen a conversation. The stated core use case is web / native app / VS Code / terminal, and one string cannot hold four. It is also not a property of the conversation — it is a property of (source, native_id) evaluated now, so a CLI syntax change staleness-bombs every row until reindex.
design: Resolve at display time from the source and native_id columns (both already present, both stable per ADR 2) via one table of open targets per source. Compare fast-resume resume_command(&self, session, yolo) -> Vec<String>: a method, computed late, and already carrying one variant axis.
acceptance_criteria: The resume_cmd column is gone from the conversations table. A reopen target is computed at display time from (source, native_id) — both already present and stable per ADR 2 — via one table of open targets per source. It returns more than one variant: at minimum a terminal command, plus web / native app / editor where the source supports them. Changing a CLI's resume syntax takes effect with no reindex. cs search --json emits the variants as structured data, not one pre-rendered string, so a GUI picks rather than parses (ADR 12).
notes:
New consumer as of 2026-07-30: 'cs pick <conv_id> --query <text>' records the selection for the query log (chat-search-6eb.22) and prints resume_cmd, so a client can pipe through it and get the string it already had with the pick recorded on the way past. cs-fzf now does exactly that.

Relevant to the redesign in two ways. It is one more caller to migrate whenever resume_cmd stops being a single frozen string. And it is probably where 'open it somewhere' belongs: the selection point is already the place that knows which conversation was chosen and is already being asked to produce a way to open it. A 'cs pick --in vscode|web|terminal' shape would satisfy this issue and the logging at once.

title: Query DSL parsed out of the search string
description: agent:claude,codex / -agent:codex / dir:!web-app / date:<3h / date:today. A TUI has one input box, so filters have to live in the query text; flags like --source do not survive the move off the CLI.
design: fast-resume query.rs is 273 lines including tests and is worth reading before writing ours. Handle the date arithmetic in civil time — adding 24h across a DST boundary lands on the wrong day.
acceptance_criteria: agent:claude,codex / -agent:codex / dir:!web-app / date:<3h / date:today all parse out of a single input string and filter results. A malformed or half-typed filter token is searched as literal text rather than erroring — mid-word is the normal state in a typeahead, so a parse error is a broken UI. Date arithmetic is civil-time, with a test proving a next-day boundary is 82,800 s across spring-forward and 90,000 s across fall-back. One parser serves both the CLI and the TUI, so filters survive the move off the CLI where --source cannot. Keystroke cost stays inside the budget on me9.1's revisit trigger.
notes:
Boundary with chat-search-6eb.26, filed 2026-07-30, since this description already names 'dir:!web-app'. They are not duplicates: this issue owns the syntax — parsing filters out of one input box, negation, multi-value — while 6eb.26 owns deriving a project name from cwd and knowing which conversations can answer at all. 'dir:' has nothing to select on until that exists, hence the dependency.

Related: the local-date rule this needs for 'date:today' and 'date:<3h' landed with chat-search-6eb.8. cs_core::time gives local_ymd and ymd_in, with chrono-tz as a dev-dependency so DST behaviour is testable off a machine in the right zone. Civil-day arithmetic (checked_add_days) is the piece still to add.

title: Native TUI
description: scripts/cs-fzf is the stopgap: fzf as a pure renderer, change:reload re-running cs search per keystroke. 8-26 ms per keystroke on a 168k-message index. A native TUI is worth ~300-400 lines and buys the 1.4-6.4 ms query cost without the cs + jq spawn.
design:
Full spec: docs/TUI-DESIGN.md (written 2026-07-29/30 after reading fast-resume v2.5.0 source). Crate boundary, layout bands and breakpoints, the row model, titles, filter surface, destinations, colour discipline and the preview pane all live there.

CRATE BOUNDARY (§1): cs-tui depends on cs-core only, entry run(db_path: PathBuf, opts) -> Result<Exit>. It never resolves the index path — cs resolves cfg.default_db() and passes it in, exposed as a `cs tui` subcommand. Ships as a subcommand rather than a separate binary so IMPORTER_VERSION stale-index detection is not duplicated per client.

Other key calls: pane reflow at width 116 rather than dropping the preview; shed Msgs before Directory when narrowing; header row + up to 3 selectable hit rows under a query, header-only in blank-query browse mode; facet bar is a projection of query state with a single source of truth; colour is layered as terminal-indexed structure / discriminable source identity / loud match highlight, never brand RGB.

The preview pane (§8) is split out as chat-search-me9.1.1 — fold model, tool traffic collapsed by default, outline mode. Coverage state in the facet bar (§5) is chat-search-me9.14.

No worker thread, generation counter or debounce — at 6 ms the search is synchronous in the event loop and there is no in-flight query to go stale. fast-resume needs all three because Tantivy plus a background rescan is genuinely async; we are not. The real work is flattening grouped results into navigable rows: our result shape is a tree and a cursor is flat, which is the cost of the better IA. Materialise a flat Vec<Row> (Header | Hit) once per search so scroll, PageDown and mouse hit-testing stay uniform.

me9.3 gates exactly one thing — the Enter action. Everything else (layout, row model, columns, filters, keymap, preview structure) is buildable without it. Wire Enter to the copy action in the meantime: `cd <dir> && <cmd>` needs no destination model and leaves no dead key.

REVISIT TRIGGER (from closing chat-search-me9.4 on 2026-07-29): the synchronous design is load-bearing on the ~6 ms query. If any keystroke path measures over ~30 ms, the search is no longer synchronous and generation numbering has to come back — reopen me9.4 rather than reinventing it. The two realistic causes are the query DSL (chat-search-6eb.11) adding parse plus multi-clause cost, and fuzzy-on-failure (chat-search-6eb.10) scanning 49,538 fts5vocab terms on a zero-hit query, which is exactly the keystroke a user is mid-word on. Measure both when they land.

SCOPE: the ~300-400 line estimate describes a list plus a search box. The acceptance criteria as written is closer to 1,200-1,800 lines (fast-resume's TUI is ~4,100, less ~550 for image support and hand-rolled syntax highlighting). Split rather than discover mid-build.
acceptance_criteria:
Runs against cs-core in-process — no cs subprocess, no jq. Typing filters as you type over the full 168k-message index with p95 keystroke-to-render under 30 ms, measured, not assumed. Grouped results are navigable with a single flat cursor that moves through conversation headers and their message hits in visual order. The header row carries the cs_core::match_density strip; hit rows expand on demand rather than always showing three (revised after chat-search-6eb.23 chose the strip over three snippets). Enter acts on the selected row via the open-target table from chat-search-me9.3, not a frozen resume_cmd string. A failed reload keeps the previous results on screen and shows the error (chat-search-me9.5) rather than rendering an empty successful search.

QUERY LOG (chat-search-6eb.22): the TUI emits no Search event per keystroke — typeahead is excluded from the log by design, and the TUI is pure typeahead. It emits exactly one Pick on Enter (finished query, conv_id, 1-based rank, shown truncated to MAX_SHOWN, n), and one Search on quit when the final query was non-blank and nothing was picked, which is the abandonment signal chat-search-6eb.21 cannot get any other way. Events go to a sink passed in by cs, not to a path the TUI resolves — see docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §1.
notes: 2026-07-30 state check. Blocked only by chat-search-me9.3, which gates the Enter destination and nothing else. Three deltas from the eval work folded into docs/TUI-DESIGN.md: (1) §1 entry signature gains a querylog sink, because queries.jsonl lives under archive_root which the TUI must not learn; (2) §3 row model revised — density strip always on, hit rows on demand; (3) §5 notes that chat-search-6eb.11 is now blocked by chat-search-6eb.26, so v1 ships facet-bar filtering without the DSL, which raises chat-search-me9.14. Workspace green at 170 tests.

title: Archive reader so layout policy never reaches importers
close_reason: Done. crates/cs-archive/src/reader.rs implements the ADR 18:393 contract: ArchiveReader::files(source_id) -> Vec<ArchivedFile> and read(&file) -> Vec<u8>, yielding (logical_path, bytes) so no importer learns whether its source was mirrored or bundled. Carries the ADR 7 determinism fix — sorts on the string form of the logical path, because Path's component-wise Ord puts <id>/subagents/x.jsonl before <id>.jsonl and a string compare does the opposite, which silently changes which file wins a metadata merge. Test files_are_returned_in_string_sorted_logical_order pins exactly that. Bundle unpacking is not implemented, but no source uses layout=bundle yet; that work is chat-search-a7k.7.

title: Claude Code importer against the real model
close_reason: Done. crates/cs-import/src/claude_code.rs (1051 lines, 28 tests) emits every cs_core::model field: the Titles fold (custom-title rename / ai-title generated / first_user), cwd and model as first-non-null with documented rationale (cwd changes mid-session in 26% of sessions; model filters the <synthetic> sentinel so an interrupted turn is not mislabelled), git_branch, surface from entrypoint, thread_key as the logical path because subagent threads share a session id (ADR 2/4), is_sidechain, and parent re-parenting to the nearest surviving ancestor so index::on_head_path never hits a dangling edge. All four Kind variants and all four Role variants are produced. head_native_id and forked_from_native_id are deliberately None — correct for an append-only CLI source per the model docs. Known remaining gap is queued_command attachments, tracked separately as chat-search-n58.13.

title: Port the PoC importers to read the archive, not live source dirs
description: They currently read ~/.codex/sessions directly, which breaks reproducibility and makes it impossible to reparse conversations that no longer exist upstream. Ordering trap: inheriting the PoC behaviour makes retroactive reparse silently not work.
close_reason: Done. crates/cs/src/query.rs:29-54 drives indexing entirely through ArchiveReader over the machine dir — reader.files(&source.id) then reader.read(f) — never ~/.codex/sessions or ~/.claude/projects. Both importers are pure functions over bytes (codex::import(logical_path, bytes), claude_code::import(logical_path, bytes)) with no filesystem access, which is what makes retroactive reparse work (ADR 1). One residue: the ChatGPT export at query.rs:63-79 is still read straight from a directory via --chatgpt-export, and that is already tracked as chat-search-6eb.7 (P0) and chat-search-a7k.8. Ordering trap 2 in docs/BACKLOG.md is discharged.

title: Source detection is frozen at cs init
description:
`detect_sources()` runs only inside `Config::default()`, and `init` refuses to run once a
config exists — so a tool installed after init is never archived and nothing ever says so.
`~/.copilot/session-state` is already on this machine (9 files, 44 KB) and is in neither the
config nor the candidate list.

The stakes are not those 9 files; it is that adopting a new agent silently starts an
unrecoverable gap, exactly as the Claude Code 30-day prune did.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `cs init` on a machine, which writes a config from whatever `detect_sources()` finds then.
2. Install or start using any agent that writes transcripts to a new location — on this
   machine, `~/.copilot/session-state` is a live example that already exists.
3. `cs archive`. The new location is not captured.
4. `cs init` again. It refuses, because a config already exists.
5. `cs status`. Nothing mentions the unconfigured location. The only signal that a gap
   started is noticing months later that the conversations are not searchable.
design: Re-detect on every cs archive and report unconfigured-but-present candidates rather than adding them silently — a source id is permanent once it enters the archive (ADR 16).
acceptance_criteria: cs archive re-runs detection on every run and reports present-but-unconfigured candidates as their own line, without adding them. ~/.copilot/session-state appears in that report on this machine. Adopting a candidate stays an explicit act (flag or config edit) because a source id is permanent once it enters the archive (ADR 16). The inverse is reported too: a source in the config whose directory has disappeared, which is the uninstalled-or-moved case and is equally silent today. Both lines survive quiet mode (chat-search-a7k.5).
notes: Confirmed live on 2026-07-30, not hypothetical: the archive at ~/.chat-archive/raw/<machine>/chatgpt-export/ held all 21 export files with matching manifest entries, while config.toml listed no chatgpt-export source at all. The source had been configured, archived, and then lost from the config — so 2,011 conversations (66% of the corpus) were archived and unreachable, and nothing said so. Re-adding the source by hand was the whole fix; no recapture was needed. This is the strongest argument for the 'source in the config whose directory has disappeared' half of the acceptance, plus its inverse: an archived source id with no config entry.

title: Recurring export reminder
description:
Every day without an export accrues unrecoverable gaps in the two server-side sources —
ChatGPT (the desktop cache is encrypted, so export is the only route) and Claude.ai
(chat-search-a7k.9, no local files at all). The existing ChatGPT export already ends
2026-07-10.

**Mechanism decided 2026-07-29: a nag line in `cs archive` output.** The archiver already
runs every 300 s under launchd, so freshness can be checked on a schedule that exists rather
than building a second one. Rejected: a desktop notification via a separate launchd job —
more moving parts for a reminder that is only actionable when you are at the machine anyway.

The nag must be **exempt from quiet mode** (chat-search-a7k.5). A staleness warning that
quiet mode suppresses is a warning that vanishes exactly when you stop reading the logs,
which is the same failure shape as the Claude Code 30-day prune: silent, and only noticed
once the data is gone.

Threshold: warn once the newest exported conversation is more than **7 days** old. That
number is a judgement call, not a measurement — it is short enough that a missed month
cannot accumulate unnoticed, and the line is cheap enough that a false nag costs nothing.
acceptance_criteria: cs archive prints a staleness line when the newest exported ChatGPT conversation is more than 7 days old, naming the source and the age in days. The line still prints on a run that captured nothing, i.e. it survives quiet mode (chat-search-a7k.5). No line at all when the export is fresh. A source with no export ever recorded warns rather than being treated as fresh — 'never exported' must not read the same as 'exported today'.

title: ChatGPT export ingest
description: 2,011 conversations, 2023-01 -> 2026-07, the single biggest chunk of the corpus and reachable no other way (the desktop app cache is encrypted). An existing export sits at ~/dev/sandbox/chat-history/data/.
design: An export is a whole-account snapshot, not an append-only file, so ADR 18's strict-superset overwrite rule does not fit: each new export reorders and rewrites, so the prefix hash changes and every export lands under _superseded/. That is the correct outcome — each snapshot is kept — but it means storage grows by a full export each time rather than by a delta, which is worth measuring before it surprises you. Dedup is therefore an importer concern keyed on the ChatGPT conversation id, not an archiver concern. The existing export at ~/dev/sandbox/chat-history/data/ is the test input; it ends 2026-07-10, which is also what makes chat-search-a7k.10 urgent.
acceptance_criteria: An export placed in the configured location is captured into the archive as an ordinary source with a permanent source id (ADR 16) and indexed by a bare 'cs index' with no flags — the --chatgpt-export flag is gone (chat-search-6eb.7). Re-running against an unchanged export captures nothing new. A newer overlapping export does not duplicate: 2,011 conversations stay 2,011, not 4,022. Conversations present in an older export but absent from a newer one are retained, because an export is a snapshot and absence from it is not deletion (ADR 9).
close_reason: Verified against the real export. chatgpt-export is an ordinary mirror source; the configured path is the directory exports unpack INTO, so each export's own Conversations__<hash>-chatgpt-NNNN/ arrives as new logical paths rather than a rewrite — every snapshot kept, nothing lands in _superseded/, and older-only conversations are retained (ADR 9). Bare 'cs index' indexes it; the --chatgpt-export flag is gone. Re-scan of an unchanged export captures nothing (21 unchanged, 0 bytes). Dedup proven empirically: two overlapping exports indexed together yield 2,011 conversation rows, not 4,022. Note the report initially SAID 4,022 — IndexStats.conversations counted objects, not rows; fixed, with IndexStats.merged now reporting re-deliveries.

title: Quiet mode for scheduled runs
description: cs archive prints a full table every run, so the log grows ~150 KB/day of "nothing changed". Only report when something was captured, or rotate.
design: Quiet by default rather than behind a --quiet flag: the scheduled launchd run is the overwhelmingly common case and it is the one generating the noise, so the default should suit it and interactive use should opt into detail. Keep the exemption list explicit and short — anything that reports a problem prints; only the 'nothing changed' table is suppressed. A warning that quiet mode can swallow is worse than a noisy log, which is the whole reason a7k.10 is called out here by name.
acceptance_criteria: A run that captures nothing prints nothing. A run that captures something prints the existing table unchanged. Idle-day log growth drops from ~150 KB to effectively zero, measured over 24 h of the live 300 s schedule. A --verbose flag restores the current always-print behaviour for debugging. Errors and the export-staleness nag (chat-search-a7k.10) are exempt and still print on an otherwise-silent run.

title: Index and search
description:
Schema, indexing and ranking. BM25 today; the open question is whether the ranking is any
good, which needs an eval set.

## Success Criteria

- Every archived source reaches the index on a default run with no flags. A source that is
  skipped says so; it never just fails to appear.
- Ranking quality is measurable. A reusable eval set exists, and the tuning constants
  (REPEAT_WEIGHT, the decay constant) have been moved against it rather than by intuition.
- A result row answers "is this the one I meant" on its own — correct local date, a title
  that is prose rather than harness machinery, and enough context to recognise the thread.
- Query latency stays inside the typeahead budget as filters and fallbacks are added:
  1.4-6.4 ms in-process today, and no keystroke path over ~30 ms (see chat-search-me9.1).
notes:
Success criterion 2 was rewritten in practice on 2026-07-30. It read: 'Ranking quality is measurable. A reusable eval set exists, and the tuning constants have been moved against it rather than by intuition.'

Still the goal. What changed is where the set comes from. Hand-authoring queries against the corpus failed for a reason worth keeping: an invented query has no information need behind it, so no result is 'the one I meant' and everything grades as vaguely useful. The harness (sheets, pooled candidates, nDCG/MRR, append-only judgements) is built and stays; the set is now to be harvested from real searches via chat-search-6eb.22 -> chat-search-6eb.21.

Until that fills up, the ranking is explicitly declared good-enough and the tuning issues are gated behind the harvested set rather than blocking anything.

title: Capture
description:
Get every conversation off the live source directories and into `~/.chat-archive` before it
is pruned, compressed or overwritten. A source id is permanent once it enters the archive
(ADR 16).

## Success Criteria

- Every transcript-writing tool on the machine is either archived or reported as a
  present-but-unconfigured candidate. Adopting a new agent cannot silently start a gap —
  that is the failure the Claude Code 30-day prune already demonstrated once.
- The two server-side sources have a routine that bounds the gap rather than a one-off
  export, and staleness is surfaced where it will actually be seen.
- The archive never loses bytes it once held: overwrite only on a strict superset, and
  preserve the prior copy under `_superseded/` when a file is rewritten or compacted.
- The scheduled run is quiet enough to read, so a genuine warning is not buried in
  ~150 KB/day of "nothing changed".

title: Interpret
description:
Parse archived transcripts into the conversation/message DAG. Importers read the archive,
never live source dirs (ADR 1).

## Success Criteria

- Format coverage is a number, not a feeling: N of M archived files parse, and the shortfall
  is attributed to named formats. A file that silently yields zero messages is a defect, not
  a gap.
- Importers stay pure functions over `(logical_path, bytes)` with no filesystem access, so
  reparsing the entire archive against a better parser is always possible.
- The DAG is sound: every `parent_native_id` names a message the importer actually emitted,
  so `index::on_head_path` never terminates early and marks live messages as abandoned.
- Titles come out as prose. No harness markup, IDE context block or slash-command expansion
  reaches a result header.
- Determinism holds: the same bytes produce the same ids and the same title, independent of
  directory enumeration order (ADR 7).

title: docs/ARCHITECTURE.md 'Current state' table is wrong in both directions
description:
Last synced 2026-07-28 and now misleading to anyone — human or agent — who reads it to decide what exists.

Says 'not built' or 'PoC only' for things that are built:
- Archive reader: listed 'not built'. crates/cs-archive/src/reader.rs exists and every importer reads through it.
- Importers Codex + Claude Code: listed 'PoC only, read live source dirs not the archive'. Both read the archive (ADR 1), and Gemini and ChatGPT export exist too, listed as 'not built'.
- Indexer + BM25: listed 'PoC only — flat messages, no DAG, no head_id, no tombstones'. All three exist.
- Clients: listed 'not built'. There is a CLI with grouped search and scripts/cs-fzf.

Also missing entirely, added 2026-07-30: ~/.chat-archive/queries.jsonl (chat-search-6eb.22). The flow diagram shows index.db as disposable and library.db as precious, and the query log is a third category the picture has no node for — precious, already real, and currently sitting beside the disposable one. Worth drawing, because it is the file whose loss actually costs something.
design: The doc says it is derived from the decision log the way index.db is derived from the archive. If that is meant literally, the fix is to regenerate rather than patch, and to decide how often. If it is aspirational, the honest move is a shorter doc that points at the code for current state and keeps only what the code cannot say.
acceptance_criteria: The 'Current state' table matches what is in crates/, or the section is removed in favour of something that cannot rot. The query log appears in the data-flow picture.

title: Ranking eval harness: sheets, pooled candidates, metrics
description: Split out from chat-search-6eb.9 so a finished deliverable is not filed under a deferred one. That issue is 'build the ranking eval SET' and is deferred pending real queries; the machinery to score any set is done and in use.
design:
cs-core/src/eval.rs holds the arithmetic only — graded relevance 0-3, nDCG@k with exponential gain, MRR, success@1/@5, exact@1, pool coverage. No I/O, so it is unit-testable and linkable by any client.

crates/cs/src/eval.rs holds the client half: 'cs eval sheet' writes one gradeable file per query, 'cs eval collect' reads the grade column back, 'cs eval run' scores.

Decisions worth not relitigating:
- A file you edit, not an interactive prompt. Relevance is comparative — whether a result is a 2 or a 1 depends on what else came back — and a one-at-a-time prompt makes that call from memory. The prompt loop was built first and deleted (183 lines).
- Candidates are pooled from three rankers (default, decay=0, repeat_weight=0), because judging only what the shipping ranker returns is how a tuning run proves the shipping ranker optimal.
- Ordered newest-first with no rank shown: rank order would anchor the judgement to the ranking being measured, and would reshuffle a half-graded file on every re-emit.
- A query with no positive judgement is unscorable, not zero, so adding a query never lowers the score.
- Grade 1 is not a hit for MRR/success@k.
- REPEAT_WEIGHT and DECAY became per-query fields on Query so the pool can vary them and 6eb.13 is a shell loop. Two tests prove each actually moves the ranking, because a sweep over a dead knob reports a flat line that reads as 'the current value is fine'.
acceptance_criteria: cs eval sheet/collect/run work end to end against a rebuilt index; metrics are unit-tested; coverage, unscorable and dangling judgements are reported as reasons to distrust the numbers.
close_reason: Landed 2026-07-30. 170 tests green across the workspace; 11 metric tests in cs-core/src/eval.rs, 8 in crates/cs/src/eval.rs, 2 proving the tuning constants actually move the ranking. Verified end to end on the real 2,963-conversation index: 24 sheets, 263 candidates, round trip through collect and run, plus the overwrite and unknown-id guards.

title: Project as a search filter
description:
From the 2026-07-30 design discussion: date and project are the strongest cues for recognising which conversation was wanted, stronger than anything in the text.

That argues for filters rather than ranking weights. A filter is predictable, debuggable and obviously wrong when it is wrong; a ranking weight is a guess with a number attached that silently trades against everything else. Date filtering is already chat-search-6eb.11's job (after:/before:); project is its natural companion and has no bead.

Available now: 940 conversations carry cwd across 99 distinct values, so the agent third of the corpus can be filtered today. ChatGPT conversations have no cwd and would fall outside any such filter, which needs saying in the UI rather than looking like missing data.
design: cwd -> project name is a cheap derivation (basename, or nearest ancestor holding .git). Derived, so ADR 16 says it must never become part of an id. Pairs with chat-search-me9.14, the facet bar that has to show coverage state rather than just non-empty sources — 'project' is exactly a facet two thirds of the corpus cannot answer.

title: Show where matches fall in a conversation, not just how many
description:
A match count alone cannot answer 'is this conversation about my query'. Three hits bunched at the start of a forty-message conversation is the subject; three at the very end is an aside raised on the way out, and the two deserve different grades and different ranks.

Not hypothetical: 86 of 147 conversations over 15 turns span more than four hours, so most long ones are several sittings across more than one topic.
design:
Group gained msg_count, prose_count and match_seqs (every match's 0-based position, not just the nested ones — 'nested' would truncate the shape to three). cs_core::match_density renders a fixed ten-cell strip, in cs-core rather than per client for the same reason as ended_date: a second implementation is a second chance to bucket it differently.

Chosen over simply showing three snippets, which gets noisy when two of the three are unrelated.
acceptance_criteria: A result carries where its matches fall as well as how many. The strip is always ten cells regardless of input, including empty, out-of-range and zero-length conversations.
close_reason: Landed 2026-07-30 as part of the sheet work. Group carries msg_count/prose_count/match_seqs; cs_core::match_density renders the strip; the eval sheet shows 'N of M prose matched' plus the strip alongside one snippet. Two synthetic tests, including the subject-vs-aside distinction and fixed width on degenerate input. Visible payoff on real data: an RL-environment query returned 'Interview Prep with Ege' with strip ·▁······▁▁, which reads as a tangent at a glance.

title: Harvest the eval set from real searches
description:
Supersedes the hand-authored approach in chat-search-6eb.9, which stalled on a real problem: a query invented by reading the corpus has no information need behind it, so nothing is 'the one I meant' and most candidates grade as vaguely useful. Judging measured the queries, not the ranking.

Logging landed 2026-07-30 (chat-search-9zk). 'cs search' records query + result ids; 'cs pick' records which conversation was opened and at what rank; 'cs needs' folds the log into one row per distinct query.

The work here is the second half: turn an accumulated log into an eval set. A picked conversation is a grade-3 with nobody grading anything, and the queries are real needs in their real distribution.
design:
Wait for data before building. Roughly 50-100 picks across 20+ distinct queries is enough to be worth converting; below that the set is thinner than the 24 hand-written queries already seeded.

Conversion is mechanical: each Need becomes a [[query]] with q = the literal text, and each picked conv_id becomes an Exact judgement in the log. Feed the result straight into 'cs eval run'.

Keep the pooled sheet flow rather than replacing it. Click data has a known position bias — a conversation can only be picked if it was shown, so a good result the ranking buried never appears as an answer, and a harvested-only set would score the current ranking as perfect by construction. Pooled judging is what covers that hole, so the two compose: harvested queries say what to ask, pooled judging says what else was there.
acceptance_criteria: 'cs eval harvest' turns the query log into a set plus judgements that 'cs eval run' scores without further editing. Queries with no pick are carried across unjudged rather than dropped, since an abandoned search is a real need the ranking failed. The generated set is distinguishable from the hand-written one, so the two can be scored separately.

title: cs index reported conversation objects, not rows
description:
IndexStats.conversations incremented once per Conversation object write_one saw, but the table is keyed on conversation.id and upserts. Any conversation delivered twice was counted twice while only one row existed.

Two ways it bit on 2026-07-30:
- Two overlapping ChatGPT exports reported 4,022 conversations for an index holding 2,011. Dedup was correct; the number made it look broken, which is the expensive kind of wrong.
- The real corpus was reported as 3,032 when the index holds 2,963 — 69 conversations span several transcript files (ADR 7) and were each counted twice. That inflated figure had already reached docs/BACKLOG.md.

Fixed as part of chat-search-a7k.8: write_one asks whether the row exists before upserting (ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE reports one changed row either way, so it cannot be inferred afterwards) and increments either conversations or the new IndexStats.merged. 'cs index' prints the merged count when non-zero, and the JSON report carries it.
acceptance_criteria: IndexStats.conversations equals the row count in the conversation table. A conversation delivered twice increments merged, not conversations. Covered by a synthetic test.
notes: Closed on arrival — filed for the record because the wrong number was published in docs/BACKLOG.md and in a7k.8's reasoning before it was caught.
close_reason: Fixed in the same change that found it. write_one now asks whether the conversation row exists before upserting and increments IndexStats.conversations or the new IndexStats.merged accordingly; 'cs index' reports merged when non-zero. Synthetic test: a_re_delivered_snapshot_is_counted_as_merged_rather_than_as_a_second_conversation. Corpus figures in docs/BACKLOG.md corrected to 2,963.

title: Facet bar must show coverage state, not just non-empty sources
description:
A source with zero indexed conversations is invisible if the facet bar is built from the index alone — the failure fast-resume ships (tui/state.rs:278-286 keeps only count > 0). A configured source whose importer threw, or whose archive run never happened, then produces a chip row that looks complete. You search, get nothing, and conclude you used a different tool, when the truth is a broken importer.

The Capture epic explicitly forbids this: a source that is skipped says so; it never just fails to appear. The facet bar is the only place in any client where the full source inventory is visible, so it is where coverage state belongs.

Build the chip row from config union index, in three states:
- configured, has rows -> normal chip with count
- configured, zero rows -> dim chip, ! marker, count 0
- detected on machine but not configured -> distinct dim style, no count (chat-search-a7k.12)

Applies to the CLI's per-source table as much as the TUI.
design: See docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §4. The chip row is a projection of query state, so a dim zero-count chip must still be selectable — clicking or Tab-cycling onto it writes agent:<source> into the query and shows an empty result set with an explanation, which is the informative outcome. Depends on cs-core exposing configured-but-unindexed sources, not just indexed ones.
acceptance_criteria: A configured source with zero indexed rows renders as a dim chip with a zero count rather than being omitted. A source present on the machine but absent from config renders in a third style. Selecting a zero-count chip produces an explained empty state, not a silent blank list.

title: Report append delta, not whole-file size, in capture byte totals
description:
An append re-captures the whole file, and the capture report bills the whole file every
time. Replaying the real manifest: 146 `appended` events reported **1176.2 MB** under the
whole-file formula against **31.8 MB** of actual new bytes — a **37x** overstatement, median
append delta 75 KB against multi-MB files. Cumulatively across 1201 capture events the
report has claimed 3411.7 MB against a 2267.3 MB live archive.

chat-search-a7k.6 made the real marginal cost *visible* — `cloned_bytes` / `copied_bytes`
now read `0.0 MB new on disk` on this reflinking machine — but did not remove the error:
`apparent_bytes` and the headline `bytes` key still bill the entire file every 300 s. Note
that allocated blocks cannot fix this either; a7k.6 measured allocated/apparent at 1.0010
over the real archive, and an APFS clone reports the source's full `st_blocks`, so no
stat-based figure sees the sharing.

Cheap to do: both `size` and `prior.fingerprint.size` are already in hand at the capture
site, so the delta is a subtraction, not new plumbing.

Matters for two reasons beyond tidiness. On any non-reflink filesystem the re-copy is real
write amplification, not a reporting artifact. And ADR 20's revisit trigger is "measured
growth exceeds 1.5 GB/month" (DECISIONS.md:543) — chat-search-4ar.2 wants to mechanise
exactly that trigger, and feeding it a 37x-inflated number would fire it on re-counted bytes
rather than on real growth.
acceptance_criteria: The capture report distinguishes new bytes from re-captured bytes: an append of 75 KB to a 5 MB file reports ~75 KB of growth, not 5 MB. Replaying the existing manifest through the new formula yields a cumulative figure that tracks the 2267.3 MB live archive rather than 3411.7 MB. The month-over-month growth number that feeds ADR 20's 1.5 GB/month trigger (and chat-search-4ar.2) is computed from the delta, so the trigger cannot fire on re-counted bytes. Existing JSON keys keep their meaning, as in chat-search-a7k.6.

title: Confirm title-fold thread ordering over multi-thread conversations
description:
For conversation claude-code:8e4aee14, the index takes first_user from the main transcript while a path-sorted walk takes it from a subagent file — Rust's Path: Ord puts '<id>/subagents/...' before '<id>.jsonl'.

This is the exact shape of a silent-corruption bug already recorded as fixed in ADR 7 (docs/DECISIONS.md:117): 'Directory enumeration order is not guaranteed and differs between runtimes... With first-write-wins, 13 conversations took a subagent's opening line as their title instead of the real name.'

Observed incidentally by the agent fixing chat-search-n58.3, whose scratch harness disagreed with the index by exactly one conversation. May be a regression, may be an artifact of that harness's own ordering rather than the indexer's — unconfirmed either way, which is why this is worth a look rather than a fix.

ADR 7 calls this class out as silent corruption: the index looks fine and contains the wrong thing.
acceptance_criteria: Either a test pinning the indexer's COALESCE/first-write order across a multi-thread conversation, or a recorded confirmation that the observed difference was the harness and not the indexer.

title: Split ranking from hydration in search_grouped
description: search_grouped pulled up to 5000 candidate messages and built a snippet for every one, then discarded all but limit x nested. message.text is by far the widest column, so a broad prefix paid for thousands of rows nobody sees. Surfaced when raising the cs-fzf result limit from 20 to 200 made typeahead unusable.
design: Ranking query selects only (msg_id, conv_id, score) and never touches message.text. A hydrate() pass then fetches full rows and builds snippets for the survivors only, via one prepared statement reused across them. Warm, at limit 200: "the" 432ms -> 79ms, "cod" 380ms -> 32ms, "code" 469ms -> 98ms, "rus" 296ms -> 38ms.
notes: The 400-800 ms figures quoted while investigating were cold-cache artifacts from re-running with different arguments; the numbers above are warmed and are the honest comparison.
close_reason: Landed in cs-core/src/search.rs: ranking query drops message.text, hydrate() fetches survivors only. 108 tests passing.

title: Record ADR 14 as decided: no daemon, clients link cs-core or spawn the CLI
description: ADR 14 (subprocess vs daemon) has been open and is listed as blocking client work. Measurements settle it: an in-process query is 1.4-6.4 ms and process spawn plus opening the 293 MB index is ~3 ms, so a daemon buys about 3 ms in exchange for a socket protocol, lifecycle management and cache-staleness bugs. Rust clients link cs-core directly; everything else spawns cs search --json at ~9 ms end to end, which fits a typeahead budget. Needs writing up in DECISIONS.md so the decision is not re-litigated.
close_reason:
Done, verified. docs/DECISIONS.md:210 now carries '## 14. Client seam: no daemon — link the core in Rust, spawn the CLI elsewhere', accepted 2026-07-29, in full house style: Context with a measurement table, three Options (resident daemon / link-and-spawn / C-ABI shared library) with honest Pro-Con bullets, Decision, Why, and a Revisit-when. design:

title: Codex legacy pre-payload format
description:
18 of the 692 archived Codex files (2.6%) predate the `payload` wrapper, and 121 prose
messages across 17 conversations are silently dropped today.

Verified against the archive on 2026-07-29, not inferred. Every `.jsonl` under `codex/` was
scanned: exactly 18 carry no `payload` key on any line and no `event_msg` anywhere. They are
**one** format, not several — chat-search-n58.16 filed the same 18 files under a
"pre-2025-09-09" boundary and was closed as a duplicate.

Shape:

- Line 1 is a session header: `{id, timestamp, instructions, git{commit_hash, branch, repository_url}}`.
- Every later line is either a bare Responses-API item — `type` of `message` (carrying
  `role` and `content`), `reasoning`, `function_call`, `function_call_output` — or the
  separator line `{"record_type":"state"}`.

The range is 2025-08-07 to 2025-12-07, so this format outlived the date any single cutover
would suggest. Recoverable prose is 58 user + 63 assistant = 121 messages across 17 files.
The 18th (`2025/08/07/rollout-2025-08-07T16-54-05-2df3f3be…jsonl`) is a header-only stub with
no messages at all — a useful edge case for the parser not to choke on.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `cs index`
2. Query for text known to be in one of the 18 files, e.g. from
   `2025/12/07/rollout-2025-12-07T17-19-51-eff5d92b…jsonl`.
3. Zero hits. The file was read and produced no messages; nothing reports that it was skipped.
design: Needs a disjoint code path gated on 'line has no payload object', which cannot regress the current format. Detect on the header line rather than per-message: line 1 having id+timestamp+git and no payload is an unambiguous format marker, so the file is classified once and dispatched, instead of every line paying a branch. The item shapes are plain Responses-API objects, so the message/reasoning/function_call mapping to Kind is the same table the current parser already has — only the unwrapping differs. Zero event_msg means there is no turn-boundary signal at all: seq comes from line order.
acceptance_criteria: All 18 legacy files import without error. 121 prose messages (58 user, 63 assistant) are indexed across 17 conversations. The header-only 2025-08-07 file yields no conversation rather than an error or an empty-titled row. The 674 payload-format files produce byte-identical index output to before the change, proven by a full reindex diff. Synthetic fixtures only — no real transcripts in the repo (chat-search-4ar.3).

title: Segment awareness: score and display by episode, keep the conversation as the unit
description:
Long conversations cover several topics, so a match count against the whole conversation cannot say what it is about. Measured 2026-07-30: 303 conversations (10%) contain an internal gap over 4 hours, which would make 757 extra segments, ~3.5 per split conversation. It lands where it should — 190 of the 303 have 6+ user turns, only 22 have 2 or fewer — and it is spread across all three sources (chatgpt 162, codex 80, claude-code 61).

The tempting move is to make the segment the retrieval unit. That should NOT be done, for a reason specific to this codebase, and this issue is the smaller thing to do instead.
design:
DECIDED: segments change scoring and display. They do not become results, and they never get ids.

Why not the retrieval unit — ADR 16 says a source id is permanent because it is embedded in every conversation id, and conv_id is source:native_id, derived from an id the source itself minted. A segment id would have to be source:native_id:n, where n comes from a boundary rule we chose and will want to tune. Change 4h to 6h and every segment id after the first altered boundary shifts. That would break eval judgements keyed on them and anything authored in library.db, and it means segment ids cannot satisfy ADR 16 while the rule stays tunable.

Two further costs of the full version: resume_cmd resumes a session, not a slice of one, so the thing shown and the thing opened would be different objects; and judgements collected against conversations become ambiguous the day the unit changes.

The smaller version keeps conv_id as identity and adds a derived message.segment column. Derived from (archive, importer version) provided the boundary rule is versioned as part of the importer, so ADR 1 holds and a rule change is an ordinary reindex.

What it buys:
- Ranking: apply REPEAT_WEIGHT within a segment instead of across the whole conversation, so a long session stops accumulating repeat-match credit from topics it is not about. This is the actual ranking defect, and it is exactly what REPEAT_WEIGHT was set by intuition to paper over.
- Display: report the matching segment's date range and turn count instead of the whole conversation's, which is what makes the match-position strip (chat-search-6eb.23) actionable rather than merely suggestive.
- Resume stays the conversation, so nothing about opening changes.

Boundary signals, best first: a cwd or git_branch change (unambiguous, but only present for the 940 agent conversations); a time gap over ~4h; lexical shift as a last resort. The gap rule is a proxy in both directions — an overnight break mid-task is not a topic change, and a mid-session pivot has no gap — which is another reason to keep it out of identity.
acceptance_criteria: Measured against the eval before adoption, not assumed. Specifically: does within-segment REPEAT_WEIGHT beat across-conversation REPEAT_WEIGHT on nDCG and success@1? If it does not, the segmentation is display-only and should say so.

title: Generated conversation summaries, and where they are allowed to live
description:
From the 2026-07-30 design discussion. A summary would help both search recall (index it alongside prose) and recognition (show it in a result row), and it is the obvious answer to 'this 40-turn conversation covers four topics and its title mentions one'.

Checked first, so nobody re-derives it: there are no free summaries to harvest. Claude Code writes 'ai-title' but the importer already uses it and it never changes within a conversation. Codex 'summary' fields are per-reasoning-block internal monologue, not conversation-level. ChatGPT export gives a title only. Anything here has to be generated.
design:
The blocking question is not how to generate them, it is where they are allowed to live.

schema.rs states the invariant: every column must be a pure function of (archive, importer version). That is what makes 'rm index.db && cs index' a valid response to any schema change, and it is why there are no migrations. An LLM summary is not a pure function — a different model, or the same model resampled, gives different text — so it cannot simply become a column without quietly voiding the rule that makes the index disposable.

Three ways out, in increasing cost:
1. library.db (chat-search-6eb.14). Correct by construction: authored, precious, backed up, and already the designated home for anything that is not derivable. Costs building library.db first.
2. A cache in index.db keyed on (conversation content hash, model id, prompt version), where a key miss means stale rather than wrong. Keeps the rebuild honest — a rebuild simply finds nothing and the column is empty until regenerated — at the cost of an explicit staleness notion the schema does not have today.
3. Regenerate on every rebuild. Purity preserved, but a full rebuild is currently ~7s and this would make it minutes and cost money, which breaks ADR 1's premise that the index is cheap to throw away.

Recommendation is (1), which makes this depend on library.db rather than race it.
acceptance_criteria: A decision recorded in DECISIONS.md about where generated text may live relative to the ADR 1 purity rule, before any summary is generated.

title: Semantic topic labels for recognising a conversation
description:
From the 2026-07-30 design discussion. The hardest part of judging a result, and of using search at all, is quickly understanding what a conversation was about. Titles help but are one line and fixed at the first turn; a long conversation that moved on is mislabelled by its own title.

Cluster-derived topic labels are one answer. Note the framing that makes this cheap to justify: wanting embeddings for DISPLAY (help me recognise this conversation) clears a much lower bar than wanting them for RANKING (chat-search-6eb.17), because a wrong label costs a glance while a wrong ranking costs the result. Do the display version first if either.
design:
Explicitly deferred until the ranking can be measured. Adding semantic retrieval before the eval works means you cannot tell whether it helped, which is the trap chat-search-6eb.9 exists to avoid.

Cheaper things to exhaust first, all of which attack the same recognition problem with no model involved: the match-position strip (chat-search-6eb.23, done), the collapsed user-message spine (see docs/TUI-DESIGN.md), and cwd-derived project names.

If it does get built, labels are derived data and cannot be a plain index.db column under ADR 1 — same purity problem as chat-search-6eb.24.
notes: Checked 2026-07-30 for free labels already in the archive: Claude Code writes 'ai-title' records, but the importer already consumes them and no conversation carries more than one distinct value, so there is no free topic-drift signal there. Codex 'summary' hits are per-reasoning-block, not conversation-level.

title: cs-archive still carries two private now_ms() copies

title: Judge the hand-authored eval set
description:
The 24 hand-written queries in evals/ranking.toml, judged. Sheets are emitted and waiting: 263 candidates across 24 queries.

Deferred, not abandoned. Judging these would produce numbers, but numbers about invented needs — see the notes for why that stalled. Kept because it is a usable stopgap if a ranking change needs measuring before the query log has filled up, and because the seed queries were checked to return at least four conversations each, so every one poses a real ranking decision.

Prefer chat-search-6eb.21. Come back to this only if something needs measuring sooner than the log allows.
acceptance_criteria: Enough of the 24 queries judged that 'cs eval run' reports coverage above 80% and a non-zero scorable count. The harness itself is chat-search-6eb.28 and is already done.
notes:
Harness landed 2026-07-30; what remains is the judging pass, which only Tyler can do.

Built:
- cs-core/src/eval.rs — graded relevance (0 irrelevant / 1 related / 2 useful / 3 exact) and the metrics: nDCG@k with exponential gain, MRR, success@1/@5, exact@1, plus pool coverage. Pure arithmetic, 11 synthetic tests, no I/O.
- crates/cs/src/eval.rs — 'cs eval judge' and 'cs eval run', 8 tests.
- evals/ranking.toml — 24 seed queries, each verified to return >= 4 conversations so it poses a ranking decision rather than a recall test. Gitignored; evals/example.toml and evals/README.md are committed.

Design decisions worth keeping:
- Two files, two lifecycles. The set is hand-written TOML the tool never rewrites, so its comments survive. Judgements are append-only JSONL, last-wins per (query id, conv id) — the same fold the archive manifest uses. Quitting a session mid-way keeps every answer already given.
- Judging pools across three rankers (default, decay=0, repeat_weight=0), not just the shipping one. Judging only what the current constants return is how a tuning run proves the current constants optimal: a conversation they bury is never seen, never judged, and counts as irrelevant for every configuration tried afterwards.
- A query with no positive judgement reports as unscorable, not as zero. Averaging a zero would make the score fall every time a query was added to the set.
- Grade 1 (related) deliberately does not count as a hit for MRR/success@k. A search that returns things about the right subject and never the conversation itself looks defensible result by result and has still failed.

Prerequisite work done to make the measurement honest: REPEAT_WEIGHT and DECAY are now per-query fields on Query rather than compile-time constants, with tests proving each actually moves the ranking — a sweep over a dead knob would report a flat line and read as 'the current value is fine'. This makes chat-search-6eb.13 a shell loop over 'cs eval run --repeat-weight'.

Known friction for the judging pass: chat-search-202 (Codex IDE context blocks in titles) makes some pooled candidates hard to read in the judge prompt. Worth fixing first if judging feels slow.

--- 2026-07-30 follow-up: judging is revisable ---
Two gaps closed after a first walkthrough of the judge loop.

'b' steps back one conversation and re-asks, showing the grade just given so it can be replaced. Mistyping a grade on the candidate you just passed was otherwise only fixable by hand-editing the JSONL mid-session.

'cs eval judge --review' walks the whole pool including already-graded conversations, showing each existing grade in the prompt; enter keeps it, a number replaces it, and nothing is appended unless the value actually changes. Default behaviour still offers only ungraded candidates, because otherwise every session after the first begins by pressing enter through all your earlier work.

Both rely on the append-only last-wins fold that was already there, so a correction is a new line and the original judgement stays visible in the file.

Testability: ask() now takes &mut dyn BufRead rather than Stdin, and candidate selection is a free function, so the key mapping and the review/default split are unit-tested rather than only smoke-tested. A mistyped key re-prompts and is never taken as a grade — 'x' silently becoming irrelevant would put a judgement in the log nobody made.

--- 2026-07-30: interactive loop dropped, replaced by sheets ---
The prompt loop was the wrong interface and is gone (183 lines). 'cs eval sheet' writes one gradeable file per query into evals/sheets/; you fill in the first column in an editor; 'cs eval collect' reads them back and appends to the same JSONL log.

Why, in order of weight:
1. Relevance is a comparative judgement. Whether a result is a 2 or a 1 depends on what else came back, and a one-at-a-time prompt makes you calibrate against memory of what already scrolled past. Seeing the whole pool at once is how the call actually gets made.
2. The prompt showed the conversation's FIRST USER MESSAGE, not the query-matched snippet — so you judged relevance against text chosen without reference to the query. Sheets carry Group.hits[0].snippet, i.e. what a real result row shows. This was a genuine defect, not just ergonomics.
3. 'b' and '--review' were ~120 lines reimplementing what a text editor does for free.

Format: a row is a grade char in column one, whitespace, then a pre-filled conv id. Everything else on the line is ignored, so notes to yourself are safe anywhere in the file. Candidates are ordered newest-first and carry NO rank — rank order would anchor the judgement to the ranking being measured (the bias pooling exists to remove) and would reshuffle a half-graded file on every re-emit.

Three guards, all tested: a grade char outside 0-3/_ is fatal rather than skipped (silently dropping it would lose a judgement actually made); a conv id the index does not hold aborts the whole collect without writing (hand-edited ids are nearly always typos, --allow-unknown escapes); and 'sheet' refuses to overwrite a file holding grades not yet collected, which is the one way this flow could lose work.

Re-emitting pre-fills every grade already in the log, so sheets/ is disposable and 'sheet' is safe to re-run after a ranking change.

Seeded state: 24 sheets, 263 candidates total. Notes in ranking.toml no longer repeat the candidate count now that the sheet header prints it.

--- 2026-07-30: deferred, and no longer blocking anything ---
Decision: the ranking is good enough to live with, so stop hand-authoring queries and collect real ones instead. Blocking edges to chat-search-6eb.13 and chat-search-6eb.12 removed; both are now free to proceed on judgement rather than waiting on a set nobody can finish honestly.

What stalled it, stated plainly so it is not rediscovered: a query invented by reading the corpus has no information need behind it. Asked which result is 'the one I meant', the honest answer is that several are fine and none is the one, because there was no one. The judging was measuring the queries, not the ranking.

The harness itself is finished and stays useful — sheets, pooled candidates, metrics, and the append-only judgement log are all what a harvested set will be scored with. What is deferred is the hand-judging pass over the 24 invented queries.

Succeeded by chat-search-6eb.21 (harvest the set from the query log). Revisit when 'cs needs' shows roughly 50-100 picks across 20+ distinct queries.

title: Theming
description: A config-file colour system for clients. Stays P4 on purpose: docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §6 decides that layer-1 structural colour comes from the terminal's indexed palette (0-15), so the user's existing terminal theme IS the theme and a bespoke system is a nicety rather than a fix. Only becomes real work if a client needs colours the 16-colour palette cannot express, or if source-identity assignments need to be user-overridable.
design: Three-layer model from docs/TUI-DESIGN.md §6: (1) structure — selection, borders, dim text, warning, accent — from the terminal's indexed palette, never hardcoded RGB, and never a full-screen background; (2) source identity from a discriminable categorical palette assigned stably per sorted source id, NOT brand colours (fast-resume proves brand colours collide: cursor and grok are both pure white, opencode and copilot near-white, in the one column whose job is telling sources apart); (3) match highlighting as the loudest thing on screen, the one place a hardcoded high-contrast pair is justified. Hard rules: nothing encoded in colour alone, respect NO_COLOR, no truecolor without COLORTERM, test on a light background before shipping.

notes:
See chat-search-6eb.24, filed 2026-07-30, for the cheaper half of this. Wanting embeddings to help recognise a conversation (topic labels in a result row) clears a much lower bar than wanting them to rank: a wrong label costs a glance, a wrong ranking costs the result. If either gets built, the display version should go first, and it can be evaluated by whether judging gets faster rather than by nDCG.

Also the sequencing constraint that applies to both: adding semantic retrieval before the ranking can be measured means there is no way to tell whether it helped.
